name: Aleppo
info: Aleppo is a city in northern Syria, on the Queiq River about 120 km from the Mediterranean, first recorded in the third millennium BCE and for centuries a trading city between the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia.

facts.founded: The city may have been inhabited since the sixth millennium BCE; Amorites occupied the area by the latter part of the third millennium BCE, when Aleppo first appears in cuneiform tablets found at Ebla and in Mesopotamia.
facts.where: On a plateau 380 m above sea level, on the Queiq River, about 120 km inland from the Mediterranean Sea, in northern Syria.
facts.known: The Amorite kingdom of Yamhad; the temple of the storm god Hadad on the citadel hill; the Hellenistic city of Beroea; the Hamdanid court of Sayf al-Dawla; the Mongol conquest of 1260; the Ottoman trade in silk; the covered souqs and khans of the old city; the battle of 2012 to 2016
facts.today: Aleppo is the capital of the Aleppo Governorate and one of the largest cities of Syria.

t: Aleppo first appears in tablets of the third millennium BCE, was the capital of the Amorite kingdom of Yamhad, and was later held by Hittites, Assyrians, Persians, Seleucids, Romans, Arabs, Mongols, Mamluks and Ottomans.

Its position on the trade routes between the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia made it, by the middle of the 16th century, the principal market in the region for goods from the east, with European consulates and the headquarters of the Levant Company.
The Suez Canal, the borders drawn after the First World War and the rise of Damascus drew trade and power away from it, and the war that reached the city in 2012 damaged much of its old city.
dyk: In 1400 Tamerlane captured Aleppo, massacred many of its inhabitants and ordered a tower of 20,000 skulls built outside the city.

sections.origins:
Aleppo lies about 120 km inland from the Mediterranean Sea, on a plateau 380 m above sea level. The city was founded a few kilometres south of the present old city, on the right bank of the Queiq River, which rises on the Aintab plateau in the north and runs south to the fertile country of Qinnasrin. The old city lies on the left bank. It was surrounded by a circle of eight hills around a prominent central hill, on which a castle was erected that had originally been a temple dating to the 2nd millennium BCE. Because the modern city occupies its ancient site, Aleppo has scarcely been touched by archaeologists.

The city may have been inhabited since the sixth millennium BCE. Excavations at Tell as-Sawda and Tell al-Ansari, just south of the old city, show that Amorites occupied the area by the latter part of the third millennium BCE. That is also when Aleppo first appears in cuneiform tablets found at Ebla and in Mesopotamia, which call it Ha-lam and speak of it as part of the Amorite state of Yamhad. Wayne Horowitz identifies it with Armi, the capital of an independent kingdom closely related to Ebla, but this identification is contested. The main temple of the storm god Hadad stood on the citadel hill, and the city was known as the city of Hadad. The name Ḥalab is believed to come from a Semitic root meaning milk, and folklore connects it with Abraham, who is said to have milked his livestock there to provide for travellers.
sections.growth:
Yamhad, also known as the land of Ḥalab (c. 1800 to 1525 BCE), was one of the most powerful kingdoms in the Near East during the reign of Yarim-Lim I, who allied with Hammurabi of Babylonia against Shamshi-Adad I. The Hittites made Aleppo a centre of worship of the Storm-God. As Beroea, it was in Late Antiquity the second largest Syrian city after Antioch, and the population of northern Syria grew under the Romans and the Byzantines well into the 5th century. Under the Hamdanid prince Sayf al-Dawla, from 944, it enjoyed a period of great prosperity and was home to the poet al-Mutanabbi and the philosopher al-Farabi. In 1128 it became the capital of the expanding Zengid dynasty.

Under the Ottomans, who found about 50,000 inhabitants in 1516, Aleppo rose to high prominence because of its position on the trade route between Anatolia and the east, at one point being second only to Constantinople in the empire. By the middle of the 16th century it had displaced Damascus as the principal market for goods coming to the Mediterranean from the east. The Levant Company of London, founded in 1581, made it its headquarters until the late 18th century, and Venice (1548), France (1562), England (1583) and the Netherlands (1613) opened consulates there. Armenian merchants developed the new quarter of Judayda. The prosperity faded after the fall of the Safavids in 1722 ended the silk caravans from Iran, and the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 hurt the economy further.
sections.rulers:
Aleppo was the capital of the Amorite dynasty of Yamhad until the Hittites under Mursili I devastated it in the 16th century BCE. About 1525 BCE a Mitanni-instigated rebellion ended the life of Yamhad’s last king, Ilim-Ilimma I, and Aleppo came under Mitanni. Suppiluliumas I conquered it in the 14th century BCE, and a dynasty of his descendants ruled until the Late Bronze Age collapse. It was later part of the Middle Assyrian Empire, of the Aramean realm of Bit Agusi and of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, and then passed to the Neo-Babylonians and the Achaemenid Persians. Alexander took it in 333 BCE, and between 301 and 286 BCE Seleucus Nicator established a Hellenic settlement there, Beroea. Tigranes of Armenia conquered Syria in 88 BCE, and in 64 BCE it became a Roman province.

Aleppo was taken by the Rashidun Muslims in 637 and was part of Jund Qinnasrin under the Umayyads. It became the seat of the Hamdanid emirate in 944 and fell to the Fatimids in 1017, and the Mirdasid dynasty ruled it from 1024 to 1080 with two Fatimid interruptions. Seljuk governors, the Zengids (from 1128) and the Ayyubids (from 1183, after Saladin) followed. The Mongols took it in 1260, the Mamluks recovered it within a month, and the Mongols took it again in 1271, 1280 and 1299. Tamerlane captured it in 1400. It became Ottoman in 1516 and the centre of the Vilayet of Aleppo in 1866. In October 1918 Prince Feisal’s forces took it, the French declared the State of Aleppo in September 1920, and in December 1924 France merged Aleppo and Damascus into a single Syrian State.
sections.life:
Because of constant invasions and political instability, the inhabitants built cell-like quarters that were socially and economically independent, each marked by the religion and ethnicity of its people. After Tamerlane’s attack in 1400, Christians who had left the city could not resettle in their old quarter, and in 1420 they founded al-Jdayde in the northern suburbs outside the walls; its inhabitants were mainly brokers between foreign traders and local merchants. The old city was enclosed by a wall with nine gates, last rebuilt by the Mamluks. Inside lay covered souqs named after crafts such as wool and copper, with khans (caravanserais) that housed traders and their goods and caeserias that served as workshops. In the medieval period, until the Mongol invasion, the city had 177 hammams.

Aleppo was a city of several faiths. In the 12th century Benjamin of Tudela recorded a Jewish community of 5,000 people. The Great Synagogue, built in the 5th century, housed the Aleppo Codex, and Sephardic Jews joined the community after the Spanish Inquisition. Armenian families and merchants had settled there since at least the 1100s, and the oldest Armenian church dates from 1491. In 1901 the population of 108,143 was 70.58 per cent Muslim, 22.66 per cent Christian, mostly Catholics, and 6.76 per cent Jewish. Armenian and Assyrian refugees arrived after the genocides of 1915. The city’s Arabic is a North Levantine dialect, and Kurdish, Turkish, Armenian and Syriac are also spoken.
sections.crises:
The Sasanian king Khosrow I pillaged and burned Aleppo in 540, and the Byzantine general Nikephoros Phokas sacked it in 962. A deadly earthquake struck on 11 October 1138; the estimates are very unreliable, but it is believed that 230,000 people died. In January 1260 the Mongols under Hulagu, with Frankish and Armenian allies, took the city: the walls fell after six days of siege and the citadel four weeks later. The Muslim population was massacred and many Jews were killed, while the Christian population was spared. In 1400 Tamerlane massacred many inhabitants and ordered a tower of 20,000 skulls built outside the city.

According to Sheikh Kamel Al-Ghazzi the population was around 400,000 before the earthquake of 1822. Cholera followed in 1823, and around 20 to 25 percent of the population died of plague in 1827. In 1850 a Muslim mob attacked Christian neighbourhoods, killing tens of Christians and looting several churches.

In August 2011 security forces shot and killed at least twelve people at anti-government protests in Aleppo. Fighting reached the city in July 2012, and by spring 2013 the Syrian Army held the west and the Free Syrian Army the east. Many parts of the Al-Madina Souq and other medieval buildings were destroyed, ruined or burnt, and the tower of the Great Umayyad Mosque was destroyed in March 2013. In 2016 government forces closed the last supply line into the east, the rebels evacuated in December, and on 22 December the army declared full control. An estimated 31,000 people were killed in Aleppo during the conflict.
sections.legacy:
The Old City, the walled city together with the old quarters outside it, covers about 350 ha. It holds covered souqs, khans, hammams, madrasas, mosques and churches in the styles of the Romans, Byzantines, Umayyads, Seljuks, Ayyubids, Mamluks and Ottomans. The Citadel stands on a mound rising 50 m above the city, and the Great Umayyad Mosque was founded about 715 by the caliph Walid I. In 1954 the French architect André Gutton proposed wide new roads, and between 1954 and 1983 many old buildings were demolished. His plan was abandoned in 1979 for one by Stefano Bianca that preserved the traditional urban fabric, and UNESCO placed the Old City on the World Heritage List in 1986.

After the First World War Aleppo lost its northern hinterland to Turkey and was separated from Mosul, and in 1939 it lost its main access to the sea when Alexandretta was annexed to Turkey. Damascus grew in importance and became the capital. In 2011 the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, the Dead Cities near Aleppo, were inscribed as a World Heritage Site. On 29 November 2024 Syrian opposition groups led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham captured the city. Aleppo is today the capital of the Aleppo Governorate, with a population of roughly two million, and reconstruction of the parts damaged in the war is under way.

summary: Aleppo, in northern Syria, first appears in tablets of the third millennium BCE and was the capital of the Amorite kingdom of Yamhad. It was ruled in turn by many powers and was a leading trading city under the Ottomans. The war of 2012 to 2016 damaged much of its old city.
notes: START: the article gives no founding date. It says Aleppo may have been inhabited since the sixth millennium BC, that Amorites occupied it by the latter part of the third millennium BC, and that the Ebla tablets (third millennium) first mention it. I used -2300 with circa true.

Only one article was available (no history file). It dates Yamhad c. 1800-1525 BC; the first Ebla record is third millennium, so the first key event is labelled '3rd millennium BCE' and the second 'c. 1800 BCE'.
SUEZ: the article says the Canal was inaugurated in 1869 (lead) and opened 1869 (Ottoman section), once '1869' in each; consistent. It also says Aleppo's decline began then.
Massacre of the Telal (1517, 9,400 Alawite men killed on Selim I's fatwa) left out: the article does not say where it happened.

Tamerlane: 'captured the city again from the Mamluks' in 1400; the article says Christians who left during the Mongol invasion could not resettle (used for al-Jdayde, 1420). The article elsewhere says Tamerlane 'invaded Aleppo in 1400 and destroyed it'; I wrote only that he massacred many and ordered the tower.

1138 earthquake: article says estimates are very unreliable, 230,000 believed dead, 'seventh deadliest in recorded history'. Kept the hedge. Also 1822 earthquake and 400,000 population come only from Al-Ghazzi as the article gives them; the article's Citadel section also says the Citadel was damaged by earthquakes, notably in 1822.
Mamluk-Mongol contests of 1260-1299 summarised; the article's Mamluk-era details (Baibars 1261, Qalawun 1281, Ain Jalut) left out for space.
Seljuk period: the article gives only Aq Sunqur as governor in 1087 and Tutush's campaigns; I wrote 'Seljuk governors' without dates.
The Armenian and Assyrian refugees 'after the genocides of 1915' follows the article's wording. Armenian refugees counted 20,007 of 156,748 in 1922; not used.

The 2011 protest deaths ('at least twelve') and the 31,000 killed in the conflict are the article's figures; the 2012 estimate of 13,500 killed by spring 2013 is from 'an international humanitarian organization' and was left out. The article's lead says 'many parts of the city suffered massive destruction'; the section on the souq says destroyed, ruined or burnt, which I followed.

The article gives 2016 as the date of the siege closing in July (government closed the last supply line July 2016) and evacuation in December; the Great Umayyad Mosque tower is given as destroyed in March 2013 (reported on 24 March 2013).

Present-day population: article says 2,098,000 estimated as of 2021; written as roughly two million without the year. The 2024 capture is stated as the article states it, no verdict. The December 2025 attack and the May 2026 tornado were left out.
Left out as not history: tourism, cuisine, sport, transport, airport, twin towns, education, municipality, climate.
Great Umayyad Mosque: the article says 'founded c. 715 by Walid I and most likely completed by Sulayman'; I give 'about 715 by the caliph Walid I'.
Dead Cities: the article says they were inscribed in 2011 as 'Ancient Villages of Northern Syria' and are in Aleppo's western suburbs; the claim that they are 'near Aleppo' follows that.
